Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 96, verses 1–5:

﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾. There are two interpretations of this. The first: its meaning is "Read the Qur'an beginning with the name of your Lord" or "seeking blessing through the name of your Lord." The phrase "in the name of your Lord" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), and that is why its implied sense is "beginning" (muftataḥan). It may mean that one begins the recitation with the words "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," or it may mean beginning with "the name of Allah" in general. The second interpretation: its meaning is "Read this utterance," and "in the name of your Lord who created" is then the object, so "in the name of your Lord" is the thing being recited.

﴿Who created﴾. The object is omitted to indicate generality, as if He said: "who created everything." Then He singled out the creation of man because of the wonders and lessons it contains. It is also possible that He meant "who created man," as He said: ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an, created man﴾ [al-Rahman: 1–3]. Then He explained it with His words ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾. "Alaq" is the plural of "alaqah," which is a drop of blood-clotted semen (nutfah min al-dam). The word "insan" here refers to the species of the children of Adam, and that is why "alaq" is in the plural, since He meant the collective. This differs from His words ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging substance﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], because there He meant each individual separately. Adam is not included in "insan" here, because he was not created from a clinging substance but from clay.

﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾. The command to read is repeated for emphasis, and the waw is circumstantial (lil-ḥāl). The purpose is to comfort the Prophet (ﷺ), as if He says: "Do what you were commanded, for your Lord is generous." The form "af'al" (the superlative pattern) here serves intensification (lil-mubālagha).

﴿Who taught by the pen﴾. This is an explanation of "the Most Generous," which indicates that the blessing of teaching is the greatest blessing. Among the forms of teaching, He singled out writing by the pen, because of what it contains of preserving sciences and the interests of religion and worldly life. Ibn al-Zubayr recited: "taught the script by the pen" (ʿallama al-khaṭṭa bil-qalam).

﴿Taught man what he did not know﴾. It may mean that this teaching is to everything without restriction. It was also said that "man" here refers to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), but the more apparent view is that it refers to the species of man in general.

﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾. This and what follows, to the end of the surah, was revealed concerning Abu Jahl some time after the beginning of the surah was revealed. He used to transgress because of the abundance of his wealth and went to extremes in his enmity towards the Prophet (ﷺ). Here, "kalla" may be a rebuke to Abu Jahl, or mean "truly", or be an opening particle. ﴿Because he sees himself as self-sufficient﴾. It is in the position of the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning: he transgresses because of his wealth. The "ru'ya" (seeing) here means knowledge, as evidenced by the verb governing the pronoun, and this only occurs with verbs of the heart. The meaning is: he knew himself to be self-sufficient, and "istaghna" is the second object. ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾. This is a threat to Abu Jahl and those like him. ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays?﴾. The commentators agree that the servant who prayed is our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and that the one who forbade him was Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him. The cause of the verse was that Abu Jahl came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was praying in the Masjid al-Haram, and he resolved to reach him and prevent him from praying. It is narrated that he said: "If I see him praying, I will certainly trample his neck." He came to him while he was praying, then turned away from him in terror. He was asked: "What is this?" He said: "A trench of fire, a terror and wings stood between me and him." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Had he come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb from limb."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 96, verses 11–14:

﴿Have you considered, if he is upon guidance,﴾ ﴿or enjoins righteousness?﴾ "Have you considered" (ʾa-raʾayta) in the matter preceding it and the one following it means: inform me. It is thus like a question that requires an answer, and it carries the sense of wonder (taʿjīb), of reproach and admonition (tawqīf), and of address (khiṭāb). The address in it may be to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to every addressee without specification. It takes two objects, and after it came the conditional particle "in" (if) in two places, namely His saying ﴿if he is upon guidance﴾ and His saying ﴿if he denies and turns away﴾. Therefore, there is need for discussion concerning the two objects of "ara'ayta" in the three places, concerning the response to the two conditionals, and concerning the pronouns attached to these verbs: "if he is upon guidance," "or enjoins righteousness," and "denies and turns away." To whom do these pronouns refer?

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying "the one who forbids" is the first object of the first "ara'ayta," and the conditional clause after it is in the position of the second object. "Ara'ayta" was repeated after that for emphasis, so it is an extra (zā'ida) that does not require an object. And His saying "Does he not know that Allah sees?" is the response to His saying "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness," addressed to the one who forbade prayer, who was Abu Jahl. Likewise the pronoun in His saying "if he denies and turns away." Its sense according to this is: Inform me about the one who forbids a servant when he prays. If this forbidder is upon guidance, or denies and turns away? Does he not know that Allah sees all his states, of guidance and error, of denial and forbidding prayer, and other things? So the purpose of the verse is a threat to him, a rebuke, and an announcement that Allah sees him.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya disagreed with him regarding the pronouns. He said: the pronoun in His saying "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness" refers to the servant who prayed, and the pronoun in His saying "if he denies and turns away" refers to the one who forbade prayer. He also disagreed with him in regarding the second "ara'ayta" as repeated for emphasis, and said: in all three places it is an admonition (tawqīf), and its response in all three places is His saying "Does he not know that Allah sees?", which suits each of them, but it came at the end of the speech for brevity (ikhtiṣār).

Al-Ghaznawi also disagreed with both of them regarding the response. He said: the response to His saying "if he is upon guidance" is omitted. He said: its estimated sense is "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness, is he not upon the truth, and is following it not obligatory?" According to this, the pronoun refers to the servant who prayed, in agreement with Ibn ʿAṭiyya.

So the purpose of the verse is a threat to him, a rebuke, and an announcement that Allah sees him.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya disagreed with him regarding the pronouns. He said: the pronoun in His saying "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness" refers to the servant who prayed, and the pronoun in His saying "if he denies and turns away" refers to the one who forbade prayer. He also disagreed with him in regarding the second "ara'ayta" as repeated for emphasis, and said: in all three places it is an admonition (tawqīf), and its response in all three places is His saying "Does he not know that Allah sees?", which suits each of them, but it came at the end of the speech for brevity (ikhtiṣār).

Al-Ghaznawi also disagreed with both of them regarding the response. He said: the response to His saying "if he is upon guidance" is omitted. He said: its estimated sense is "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness, is he not upon the truth, and is following it not obligatory?" According to this, the pronoun refers to the servant who prayed, in agreement with Ibn ʿAṭiyya.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 96, verses 11–14:

﴿Have you considered, if he is upon guidance,﴾ ﴿or enjoins righteousness?﴾ "Have you considered" (ʾa-raʾayta) in the matter preceding it and the one following it means: inform me. It is thus like a question that requires an answer, and it carries the sense of wonder (taʿjīb), of reproach and admonition (tawqīf), and of address (khiṭāb). The address in it may be to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to every addressee without specification. It takes two objects, and after it came the conditional particle "in" (if) in two places, namely His saying ﴿if he is upon guidance﴾ and His saying ﴿if he denies and turns away﴾. Therefore, there is need for discussion concerning the two objects of "ara'ayta" in the three places, concerning the response to the two conditionals, and concerning the pronouns attached to these verbs: "if he is upon guidance," "or enjoins righteousness," and "denies and turns away." To whom do these pronouns refer?

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying "the one who forbids" is the first object of the first "ara'ayta," and the conditional clause after it is in the position of the second object. "Ara'ayta" was repeated after that for emphasis, so it is an extra (zā'ida) that does not require an object. And His saying "Does he not know that Allah sees?" is the response to His saying "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness," addressed to the one who forbade prayer, who was Abu Jahl. Likewise the pronoun in His saying "if he denies and turns away." Its sense according to this is: Inform me about the one who forbids a servant when he prays. If this forbidder is upon guidance, or denies and turns away? Does he not know that Allah sees all his states, of guidance and error, of denial and forbidding prayer, and other things? So the purpose of the verse is a threat to him, a rebuke, and an announcement that Allah sees him.

He said: the pronoun in His saying "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness" refers to the servant who prayed, and the pronoun in His saying "if he denies and turns away" refers to the one who forbade prayer. Al-Ghaznawi also disagreed with both of them regarding the response. He said: the response to His saying "if he is upon guidance" is omitted. He said: its estimated sense is "if he is upon guidance or enjoins righteousness, is he not upon the truth, and is following it not obligatory?" According to this, the pronoun refers to the servant who prayed, in agreement with Ibn ʿAṭiyya.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 96, verse 15–19:

﴿Indeed, if he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾. He threatened Abu Jahl that if he did not desist from his disbelief and transgression, he would be seized by the forelock and cast into the Fire. The nasiyah (forelock) is the front part of the head, and this is like His saying: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. Al-safa' here means to drag and to grasp a thing, and it was said that it means to burn, from your saying "the fire scorched him" (safa'thu al-nar). The emphasis in "la-nasfa'an" is by the lam and the light nun, and it was written in the Mushaf with an alif in observance of pause. It appears to me that this threat was carried out against him on the day of Badr, when he was killed and seized by the forelock and dragged to the well.

﴿A lying, sinning forelock﴾. The forelock is replaced by (badal) the forelock, and describing it with lying and sin is a figurative usage (tajawwuz); the liar and the sinner in reality is its owner. The khati' (sinner) is one who commits a sin deliberately, while the mukhti' (one who errs) is one who commits it without intention.

﴿Then let him call upon his council﴾. The nadi and al-nadi (council) is the assembly in which people gather. Abu Jahl had said: "Does Muhammad threaten me? By God, there is no one in this valley with a greater council than mine." So the verse was revealed as a threat and a challenge to him. The meaning is: let him call upon the people of his council to support him, if they are able to do so. Then He threatened him that He would summon for him the Zabaniyah of Hell, who are the angels appointed over the punishment. The Zabaniyah, linguistically, their singular is zabaniyah, and it was said zabani. In a hadith, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If he had called upon his council, the Zabaniyah would have seized him openly."

﴿And prostrate yourself and draw near﴾. That is, draw near to God through prostration, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating, so strive in supplication." This is a place of prostration according to al-Shafi'i, and it is not among the obligatory prostrations (a'zaim al-sujud) according to Malik.
